content: In Raft, leader election is initiated when a follower node experiences an election timeout without receiving heartbeats. Followers increment their currentTerm and transition to the candidate state, immediately voting for themselves and sending RequestVote RPCs to all peers in the cluster.

To prevent split votes among competing candidates, Raft utilizes randomized election timeouts chosen uniformly from a range of 150ms to 300ms. A candidate wins an election if it receives votes from a strict majority of servers in the cluster for the same term.

Once a leader is elected, it begins servicing client requests. Each client request contains a command to be executed by the replicated state machines. The leader appends the command to its log as a new entry and issues AppendEntries RPCs in parallel to all other servers to replicate the entry.

Raft maintains the Log Matching Property: if two entries in different logs have the same index and term, then they store the same command, and their logs are identical in all preceding entries up to that index. Leaders never overwrite or truncate their own logs.

Configuration changes use a two-phase joint consensus approach. Joint consensus allows individual servers to transition between configurations at different times without compromising safety. During joint consensus, log entries are committed under both old and new configurations simultaneously.

Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs structure high-dimensional vector embeddings into multi-layer proximity graphs. The top layer has the longest link lengths and sparsest connections, acting as a geometric skip-list, while layer 0 contains all vectors connected to their nearest neighbors.

The parameter M defines the maximum number of bidirectional connections per element per layer, typically set between 16 and 64. The efConstruction parameter controls the size of the dynamic candidate list during graph building; higher values increase indexing recall at the cost of slower build times.

During query routing, efSearch controls the priority queue depth when traversing layer 0. Increasing efSearch improves retrieval recall with sub-linear latency trade-offs, enabling high throughput while avoiding full distance scans across the entire corpus.

HNSW graphs maintain connections in memory alongside vector coordinates. For 768-dimensional float32 embeddings, each vector requires approximately 3KB for the raw coordinates plus 1KB to 2KB for neighbor pointer lists depending on M, necessitating RAM-optimized indexing instances.

Unlike IVFFlat which relies on coarse quantization centroids and inverted lists, HNSW preserves exact vector coordinates and relies on small-world graph navigation. This achieves significantly higher Recall@k on high-dimensional dense embeddings without requiring periodic index retrain phases.

PostgreSQL full-text search converts raw unstructured document strings into the tsvector data type. A tsvector represents a sorted list of distinct normalized lexemes, stripped of capitalization, punctuation, and English stopwords according to the active text search dictionary.

The websearch_to_tsquery function parses natural user search expressions without throwing syntax errors on unclosed quotes or operators. It understands boolean AND by default, OR operators, minus signs for negation, and quoted phrases as adjacent phrase matching with the FOLLOWED BY (<->) operator.

Generalized Inverted Indexes (GIN) provide efficient lexical lookup for tsvector columns. GIN indexes store individual lexemes as keys, each mapped to a posting list of tuple IDs (TIDs). Multi-word search performs fast bitmap AND intersections across posting lists.

The ts_rank function computes relevance scores based on lexeme frequency (TF). It rewards documents where query terms appear multiple times and takes into account term density and document length normalization, with options to penalize long documents logarithmically.

Storing tsvector as a GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector("english", content)) STORED column avoids runtime parsing overhead during search queries. The GIN index updates automatically in the same transaction as row insertions or updates without triggers.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) scores each document d across retrieval lists using RRF(d) = sum(1 / (k + r_i(d))), where r_i(d) is the 1-based rank of d in retrieval strategy i, and k is a constant parameter conventionally set to 60 to smooth rank disparity.

section: Combining Dense Vector and Lexical BM25 Search
content: Combining PostgreSQL tsvector full-text search with Gemini dense vector embeddings via RRF mitigates individual failure modes. Lexical search reliably catches exact identifiers, codes, and acronyms, while dense semantic retrieval matches paraphrased concepts and high-level technical intent.

Following RRF fusion of top-25 lexical and top-25 dense candidates, a listwise reranker evaluates the top-20 merged candidates. The reranker computes fine-grained cross-attention scores between the query and candidate passages, producing the final calibrated top-5 context window.

When maximum candidate similarity drops below the calibrated relevance threshold (0.58 dense similarity or 0.08 lexical score), the retrieval pipeline abstains from answer generation. This zero-trust boundary prevents model hallucinations on out-of-domain or unanswerable enterprise inquiries.

First-stage hybrid retrieval finishes in under 25 milliseconds via indexed PostgreSQL queries. Reranking adds 30ms to 70ms of inference latency, providing an optimal balance between retrieval accuracy (MRR > 0.95) and real-time streaming user experience.

PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (RLS) restricts row access at the database engine level. By defining policies using tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting("app.tenant_id", true), "")::uuid, every SQL query automatically filters rows to the authenticated tenant, even when application queries omit WHERE clauses.

Neon uses PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode. Setting session parameters via SET can leak across pooled connections. To guarantee safety, all tenant scoping must execute SELECT set_config("app.tenant_id", $1, true) where is_local=true ensures settings revert on transaction commit or rollback.

Password authentication uses Argon2id with memory cost of 64MB (65536 KiB), time cost of 3 iterations, and parallelism of 4 threads. Argon2id provides state-of-the-art resistance against both side-channel cache attacks and GPU-accelerated brute-force attacks.

section: JWT Access and Revocable Refresh Tokens
content: DocSage implements 15-minute short-lived JWT access tokens alongside rotating 7-day refresh tokens. Refresh tokens are stored in PostgreSQL as SHA-256 hashes and delivered exclusively via httpOnly, secure, SameSite cookies. Refreshing rotates the token and revokes previous tokens.

The audit_log table provides an append-only ledger recording actor_id, action, entity, entity_id, metadata, and UTC timestamp. The application database user lacks UPDATE and DELETE privileges on audit_log to guarantee tamper-proof auditability for compliance.

When sending an AppendEntries RPC, the leader includes the index and term of the entry immediately preceding the new entries in its log (prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm). In production deployment: This inductive log matching invariant prevents committed entries from ever being modified or deleted in any valid Raft state. [Ref: Raft Consensus Algorithm Specification, Chapter 6, Paragraph 2].

If the follower does not find an entry in its log with the matching index and term, it rejects the new entries. In production deployment: Upon rejecting an AppendEntries RPC, the follower sends an error status, causing the leader to decrement nextIndex for that follower and retry. [Ref: Raft Consensus Algorithm Specification, Chapter 6, Paragraph 3].

The consistency check serves as an induction step: the leader log and follower log must match at prevLogIndex for subsequent entries to be safely appended. In production deployment: Optimized rejection recovery allows followers to send the term and first index of the conflicting term, bypassing one-by-one index decrementing. [Ref: Raft Consensus Algorithm Specification, Chapter 6, Paragraph 4].

section: Cluster Membership Changes and Joint Consensus (Part 6)
content: Configuration changes cannot switch directly from old configuration C_old to new configuration C_new because conflicting majorities could elect separate leaders. In production deployment: During the joint consensus window, an election requires independent majorities from both the original C_old membership and the incoming C_new membership. [Ref: Raft Consensus Algorithm Specification, Chapter 33, Paragraph 2].

section: Cluster Membership Changes and Joint Consensus (Part 7)
content: Joint consensus entry C_old,new is logged and committed under both C_old and C_new independent majority rules. In production deployment: Removing servers can cause disturbances if removed servers timeout and send RequestVote RPCs; Raft mitigates this with minimum lease intervals. [Ref: Raft Consensus Algorithm Specification, Chapter 33, Paragraph 3].

section: Cluster Membership Changes and Joint Consensus (Part 8)
content: Once C_old,new is committed on the leader, the leader logs entry C_new and replicates it across the new cluster configuration. In production deployment: Servers not in the active configuration do not count toward majority quorums, but may act as non-voting catchup members before joining. [Ref: Raft Consensus Algorithm Specification, Chapter 33, Paragraph 4].

section: Cluster Membership Changes and Joint Consensus (Part 1)
content: Servers immediately adopt configuration entries upon appending them to their local logs without waiting for commitment. In production deployment: During the joint consensus window, an election requires independent majorities from both the original C_old membership and the incoming C_new membership. [Ref: Raft Consensus Algorithm Specification, Chapter 33, Paragraph 5].

Practical systems cannot allow logs to grow without bound; Raft uses memory snapshotting where each server writes its state to persistent disk. In production deployment: InstallSnapshot chunks are sent in sequential byte offsets, and followers assemble them into a staging file before verifying checksums. [Ref: Raft Consensus Algorithm Specification, Chapter 46, Paragraph 2].

A snapshot includes the state machine data, the lastIncludedIndex, and the lastIncludedTerm of the most recent committed log entry applied. In production deployment: Upon receiving a valid InstallSnapshot, the follower discards any existing log entries preceding lastIncludedIndex and resets its state machine. [Ref: Raft Consensus Algorithm Specification, Chapter 46, Paragraph 3].

All log entries up to lastIncludedIndex are discarded from memory and disk once the snapshot file is atomically fsynced. In production deployment: Snapshotting introduces copy-on-write overhead; implementations fork a background worker to avoid blocking ongoing consensus requests. [Ref: Raft Consensus Algorithm Specification, Chapter 46, Paragraph 4].

section: Full Text Search tsvector and GIN Inverted Indexes (Part 6)
content: PostgreSQL full-text search processes raw text into a sorted collection of lexemes stored as a tsvector data type. In production deployment: The Snowball stemming algorithm reduces inflected words to their root linguistic form, enabling morphological retrieval. [Ref: PostgreSQL 16 Internals and Security Architecture, Chapter 32, Paragraph 2].

section: Full Text Search tsvector and GIN Inverted Indexes (Part 7)
content: The GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) index stores an inverted entry for each lexeme pointing to a bitmap posting list of tuple identifiers (TIDs). In production deployment: Stopwords defined in the english dictionary (e.g. the, is, at) are stripped during tsvector generation to optimize index storage. [Ref: PostgreSQL 16 Internals and Security Architecture, Chapter 33, Paragraph 3].

section: Full Text Search tsvector and GIN Inverted Indexes (Part 8)
content: Search queries use tsquery operators: & (AND), | (OR), ! (NOT), and <-> (FOLLOWED BY phrase proximity search). In production deployment: ts_rank and ts_rank_cd calculate lexical relevance based on term frequency and document length normalization factors. [Ref: PostgreSQL 16 Internals and Security Architecture, Chapter 33, Paragraph 4].

section: Full Text Search tsvector and GIN Inverted Indexes (Part 1)
content: GIN indexes support fast multi-lexeme lookups because posting lists can be combined via bitwise AND and OR bitmap operations. In production deployment: The Snowball stemming algorithm reduces inflected words to their root linguistic form, enabling morphological retrieval. [Ref: PostgreSQL 16 Internals and Security Architecture, Chapter 33, Paragraph 5].

section: Concurrency Control and MVCC Tuple Visibility (Part 6)
content: Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) in PostgreSQL ensures readers never block writers and writers never block readers. In production deployment: Updating a tuple writes a complete new tuple version to disk and updates the xmax of the original tuple to the current transaction ID. [Ref: PostgreSQL 16 Internals and Security Architecture, Chapter 46, Paragraph 2].

section: Concurrency Control and MVCC Tuple Visibility (Part 7)
content: Each table tuple contains header attributes: xmin (transaction that inserted the row) and xmax (transaction that updated or deleted it). In production deployment: VACUUM processes dead tuples whose xmax is older than the oldest active transaction snapshot, reclaiming dead disk space. [Ref: PostgreSQL 16 Internals and Security Architecture, Chapter 46, Paragraph 3].

section: Concurrency Control and MVCC Tuple Visibility (Part 8)
content: A transaction visibility snapshot records the active transaction IDs at snapshot creation, determining which tuple versions are visible. In production deployment: HOT (Heap-Only Tuples) optimization avoids updating index pointers when a tuple is updated within the same 8KB disk page without key changes. [Ref: PostgreSQL 16 Internals and Security Architecture, Chapter 46, Paragraph 4].

section: Concurrency Control and MVCC Tuple Visibility (Part 1)
content: In READ COMMITTED isolation mode, each SQL statement creates a fresh snapshot, whereas REPEATABLE READ holds a single snapshot for the transaction. In production deployment: Updating a tuple writes a complete new tuple version to disk and updates the xmax of the original tuple to the current transaction ID. [Ref: PostgreSQL 16 Internals and Security Architecture, Chapter 46, Paragraph 5].

section: pgvector Index Architecture: HNSW vs IVFFlat (Part 6)
content: pgvector extends PostgreSQL with native vector data types and distance operators: <-> (L2), <#> (inner product), and <=> (cosine). In production deployment: Cosine distance in pgvector computes 1 - (A dot B) / (norm(A) * norm(B)); pre-normalizing vectors to unit length enables faster inner product operations. [Ref: PostgreSQL 16 Internals and Security Architecture, Chapter 59, Paragraph 2].

section: pgvector Index Architecture: HNSW vs IVFFlat (Part 7)
content: HNSW indexes create hierarchical navigable graphs providing higher Recall@k at low query latencies without requiring retraining. In production deployment: Iterative index scans in pgvector allow queries combining vector similarity with SQL WHERE filters to retrieve valid matches efficiently. [Ref: PostgreSQL 16 Internals and Security Architecture, Chapter 59, Paragraph 3].

section: pgvector Index Architecture: HNSW vs IVFFlat (Part 8)
content: IVFFlat partitions vector space into Voronoi cells using k-means clustering; queries probe the closest lists specified by probes parameter. In production deployment: Memory allocation for HNSW graph traversal is governed by work_mem; insufficient work_mem causes spills to temporary disk buffers. [Ref: PostgreSQL 16 Internals and Security Architecture, Chapter 59, Paragraph 4].

section: pgvector Index Architecture: HNSW vs IVFFlat (Part 1)
content: HNSW construction requires tuning m (max connections) and ef_construction (candidate list size), balancing index speed with build time. [Ref: PostgreSQL 16 Internals and Security Architecture, Chapter 60, Paragraph 5].

section: Cryptographic Key Schedule and Secret Derivation (Part 6)
content: TLS 1.3 key derivation is structured around HKDF (HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function, RFC 5869). In production deployment: Key updates execute by calling HKDF-Expand-Label on the current traffic secret, providing forward secrecy without renegotiating. [Ref: RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 Protocol Specification, Chapter 15, Paragraph 2].

section: Cryptographic Key Schedule and Secret Derivation (Part 7)
content: The key schedule progresses through three phases: Early Secret, Handshake Secret, and Master Secret. In production deployment: The exporter master secret provides cryptographically isolated keys for application-level protocols such as WebRTC and HTTP/2. [Ref: RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 Protocol Specification, Chapter 15, Paragraph 3].

section: Cryptographic Key Schedule and Secret Derivation (Part 8)
content: HKDF-Extract combines input keying material with salt, while HKDF-Expand-Label generates specialized traffic keys and nonces. In production deployment: Zero-Round-Trip (0-RTT) early data uses early_traffic_secret derived from pre-shared keys before ServerHello arrives. [Ref: RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 Protocol Specification, Chapter 15, Paragraph 4].

section: Cryptographic Key Schedule and Secret Derivation (Part 1)
content: Traffic keys for application data are derived from client_application_traffic_secret_0 and server_application_traffic_secret_0. In production deployment: Key updates execute by calling HKDF-Expand-Label on the current traffic secret, providing forward secrecy without renegotiating. [Ref: RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 Protocol Specification, Chapter 15, Paragraph 5].

0-RTT allows clients resuming a connection to transmit application data alongside the initial ClientHello, cutting latency to 0-RTT. In production deployment: If a server cannot verify freshness of 0-RTT data, it sends an early data rejection, forcing the client to retransmit after 1-RTT. [Ref: RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 Protocol Specification, Chapter 28, Paragraph 2].

Because 0-RTT data is encrypted under a static pre-shared key secret, it is susceptible to network replay attacks by passive observers. In production deployment: Early data cannot achieve forward secrecy against an attacker who compromises the pre-shared key at a future date. [Ref: RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 Protocol Specification, Chapter 28, Paragraph 3].

Servers must strictly restrict 0-RTT to idempotent HTTP requests (e.g. GET queries without side effects) to avoid duplicate execution. In production deployment: Modern HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 implementations mandate client opt-in flags for 0-RTT data paths to safeguard stateful endpoints. [Ref: RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 Protocol Specification, Chapter 28, Paragraph 4].

Anti-replay mechanisms include Single-Use Tickets, Client Hello Ticket Age checks, and distributed timestamp sliding windows. section: Record Layer Encryption and AEAD Ciphers (Part 6)
content: TLS 1.3 mandates Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) algorithms: AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, and ChaCha20-Poly1305. In production deployment: Each record is assigned a monotonic 64-bit sequence number that is never transmitted on the wire but XORed into the AEAD nonce. [Ref: RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 Protocol Specification, Chapter 41, Paragraph 2].

section: Record Layer Encryption and AEAD Ciphers (Part 7)
content: Static cipher suites and CBC-mode ciphers vulnerable to padding oracle attacks (e.g. Lucky Thirteen) are completely banned. In production deployment: Record padding allows endpoints to obscure message sizes against traffic analysis attacks by appending variable trailing zeroes. [Ref: RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 Protocol Specification, Chapter 42, Paragraph 3].

section: Record Layer Encryption and AEAD Ciphers (Part 8)
content: The TLS record header consists of an opaque content type (always 23 / application_data), protocol version (0x0303), and payload length. In production deployment: Maximum plaintext record length is bounded at 2^14 bytes (16384 bytes) to prevent buffer exhaustion and latency amplification. [Ref: RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 Protocol Specification, Chapter 42, Paragraph 4].

section: Record Layer Encryption and AEAD Ciphers (Part 1)
content: The true content type (handshake, alert, or application data) is placed inside the encrypted payload before AEAD tagging. In production deployment: Each record is assigned a monotonic 64-bit sequence number that is never transmitted on the wire but XORed into the AEAD nonce. [Ref: RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 Protocol Specification, Chapter 42, Paragraph 5].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
section: Binary Framing Layer and Frame Types (Part 6)
content: HTTP/2 replaces textual newline-delimited protocol formats with an optimized 9-byte binary framing layer. In production deployment: RST_STREAM terminates an individual stream immediately without impacting concurrent streams on the same connection. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 1, Paragraph 2].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
section: Binary Framing Layer and Frame Types (Part 7)
content: Frame headers contain a 24-bit payload length, 8-bit frame type, 8-bit flag field, and 31-bit stream identifier. In production deployment: The SETTINGS frame negotiates maximum concurrent streams, initial window size, and header table capacity upon connection startup. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 1, Paragraph 3].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
section: Binary Framing Layer and Frame Types (Part 8)
content: Standard frame types include DATA (0x0), HEADERS (0x1), PRIORITY (0x2), RST_STREAM (0x3), SETTINGS (0x4), and GOAWAY (0x7). In production deployment: PING frames measure round-trip times and verify connection liveness; receivers must echo the payload with the ACK flag set. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 1, Paragraph 4].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
section: Binary Framing Layer and Frame Types (Part 1)
content: Interleaving frames from multiple independent streams across a single TCP connection solves client-side connection limits. In production deployment: RST_STREAM terminates an individual stream immediately without impacting concurrent streams on the same connection. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 1, Paragraph 5].

content: Standard frame types include DATA (0x0), HEADERS (0x1), PRIORITY (0x2), RST_STREAM (0x3), SETTINGS (0x4), and GOAWAY (0x7). In production deployment: PING frames measure round-trip times and verify connection liveness; receivers must echo the payload with the ACK flag set. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 4, Paragraph 5].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
section: Binary Framing Layer and Frame Types (Part 1)
content: Interleaving frames from multiple independent streams across a single TCP connection solves client-side connection limits. In production deployment: RST_STREAM terminates an individual stream immediately without impacting concurrent streams on the same connection. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 4, Paragraph 1].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
section: Binary Framing Layer and Frame Types (Part 2)
content: HTTP/2 replaces textual newline-delimited protocol formats with an optimized 9-byte binary framing layer. In production deployment: RST_STREAM terminates an individual stream immediately without impacting concurrent streams on the same connection. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 4, Paragraph 2].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
section: Binary Framing Layer and Frame Types (Part 3)
content: Frame headers contain a 24-bit payload length, 8-bit frame type, 8-bit flag field, and 31-bit stream identifier. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 4, Paragraph 3].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
content: HTTP/2 utilizes HPACK (RFC 7541) to compress repetitive request and response headers across concurrent streams. In production deployment: The dynamic table size is constrained by SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE to prevent denial-of-service memory exhaustion on proxies. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 14, Paragraph 2].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
content: HPACK maintains a static table of 61 pre-defined header name-value pairs and a dynamic FIFO table populated by connection traffic. In production deployment: Headers containing sensitive secrets (e.g. Authorization or Cookie) use the "never indexed" flag to prevent CRIME/BREACH compression leakage. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 14, Paragraph 3].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
content: Header fields can be represented as indexed integers, literal representations with indexing, or literal representations without indexing. In production deployment: In HTTP/3, HPACK is replaced by QPACK to prevent head-of-line blocking across independent streams on QUIC transport. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 14, Paragraph 4].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
content: String literals in HPACK are compressed using a static Huffman code table optimized for HTTP character distribution frequencies. In production deployment: The dynamic table size is constrained by SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE to prevent denial-of-service memory exhaustion on proxies. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 15, Paragraph 5].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
content: HTTP/2 utilizes HPACK (RFC 7541) to compress repetitive request and response headers across concurrent streams. In production deployment: The dynamic table size is constrained by SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE to prevent denial-of-service memory exhaustion on proxies. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 15, Paragraph 1].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
content: HPACK maintains a static table of 61 pre-defined header name-value pairs and a dynamic FIFO table populated by connection traffic. In production deployment: Headers containing sensitive secrets (e.g. Authorization or Cookie) use the "never indexed" flag to prevent CRIME/BREACH compression leakage. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 15, Paragraph 2].

documentTitle: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture
content: Header fields can be represented as indexed integers, literal representations with indexing, or literal representations without indexing. In production deployment: In HTTP/3, HPACK is replaced by QPACK to prevent head-of-line blocking across independent streams on QUIC transport. [Ref: RFC 7540 & 9113 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Transport Architecture, Chapter 15, Paragraph 3].

section: Refresh Token Rotation and Revocation Architecture (Part 6)
content: Refresh tokens permit clients to obtain fresh short-lived access tokens without forcing end-users to re-authenticate credentials. In production deployment: Refresh token cookies must be marked with httpOnly, secure, and SameSite=Strict/Lax flags to prevent XSS script extraction. documentTitle: RFC 6749 OAuth 2.0 and RFC 7519 JWT Architecture
section: Refresh Token Rotation and Revocation Architecture (Part 7)
content: Refresh token rotation issues a new refresh token with each refresh request while immediately invalidating the prior token. In production deployment: Revocation endpoints (RFC 7009) allow clients to explicitly invalidate refresh tokens upon user logout. [Ref: RFC 6749 OAuth 2.0 and RFC 7519 JWT Architecture, Chapter 28, Paragraph 3].

documentTitle: RFC 6749 OAuth 2.0 and RFC 7519 JWT Architecture
section: Refresh Token Rotation and Revocation Architecture (Part 8)

content: Refresh tokens permit clients to obtain fresh short-lived access tokens without forcing end-users to re-authenticate credentials. In production deployment: Refresh token cookies must be marked with httpOnly, secure, and SameSite=Strict/Lax flags to prevent XSS script extraction. [Ref: RFC 6749 OAuth 2.0 and RFC 7519 JWT Architecture, Chapter 33, Paragraph 4].

documentTitle: RFC 6749 OAuth 2.0 and RFC 7519 JWT Architecture
section: Refresh Token Rotation and Revocation Architecture (Part 7)
content: Refresh token rotation issues a new refresh token with each refresh request while immediately invalidating the prior token. [Ref: RFC 6749 OAuth 2.0 and RFC 7519 JWT Architecture, Chapter 33, Paragraph 5].

documentTitle: NIST SP 800-63B Authentication and Lifecycle Management
content: NIST SP 800-63B mandates minimum password lengths of at least 8 characters, recommending support for up to 64 characters. In production deployment: Verifiers must permit users to use password managers by allowing paste operations in all password input fields. [Ref: NIST SP 800-63B Authentication and Lifecycle Management, Chapter 1, Paragraph 2].

documentTitle: NIST SP 800-63B Authentication and Lifecycle Management
content: Arbitrary password composition rules (requiring uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols) are deprecated due to poor user outcomes. In production deployment: Password hints and knowledge-based authentication questions (e.g. mothers maiden name) are disallowed due to vulnerability to social engineering. [Ref: NIST SP 800-63B Authentication and Lifecycle Management, Chapter 1, Paragraph 3].

documentTitle: NIST SP 800-63B Authentication and Lifecycle Management
content: Periodic arbitrary password expiration (e.g. forced 90-day password changes) is explicitly prohibited unless compromise is suspected. In production deployment: Credential stuffing defense requires rate limiting, CAPTCHA challenges, and IP reputation heuristics on login endpoints. [Ref: NIST SP 800-63B Authentication and Lifecycle Management, Chapter 1, Paragraph 4].

documentTitle: NIST SP 800-63B Authentication and Lifecycle Management
content: Verifiers must screen prospective passwords against lists of compromised, leaked, or commonly used dictionary passwords. In production deployment: Verifiers must permit users to use password managers by allowing paste operations in all password input fields. [Ref: NIST SP 800-63B Authentication and Lifecycle Management, Chapter 2, Paragraph 5].

content: Verifiers must store passwords using approved salted, memory-hard cryptographic hash functions: Argon2id, scrypt, or PBKDF2. documentTitle: NIST SP 800-63B Authentication and Lifecycle Management
content: Argon2id combines Argon2d (data-dependent memory access) and Argon2i (data-independent memory access) to defend against side-channel attacks. In production deployment: When legacy systems transition from SHA-1 or MD5, passwords should be transparently upgraded to Argon2id upon next successful login. [Ref: NIST SP 800-63B Authentication and Lifecycle Management, Chapter 15, Paragraph 3].

documentTitle: NIST SP 800-63B Authentication and Lifecycle Management
content: Recommended Argon2id production parameters: minimum memory cost of 64MB (65536 KiB), time cost of 3 iterations, and parallelism of 4. [Ref: NIST SP 800-63B Authentication and Lifecycle Management, Chapter 15, Paragraph 4].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
content: [DEPRECATED SPECIFICATION] In early Raft Draft v0.9, randomized election timeouts were specified between 100ms and 200ms. In production deployment: Modern Raft implementations reject Draft v0.9 timeout values because 100ms-200ms proved too narrow for wide-area broadcast heartbeats. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 1, Paragraph 2].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
content: [SUPERSEDED] Draft v0.9 explored single-server cluster transitions without formal joint consensus intermediate states. In production deployment: This archival draft is retained exclusively for comparative distributed consensus research and regression testing. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 1, Paragraph 3].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
content: [HISTORICAL] Early draft formulations permitted followers to truncate uncommitted entries before receiving leader match confirmations. In production deployment: Do not apply Draft v0.9 configurations in production distributed state machine clusters. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 1, Paragraph 4].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
content: [CONFLICTING MODEL] Draft v0.9 lacked the formal Pre-Vote extension, resulting in disruptions when partitioned nodes rejoined. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 1, Paragraph 5].

In production deployment: Modern Raft implementations reject Draft v0.9 timeout values because 100ms-200ms proved too narrow for wide-area broadcast heartbeats. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 3, Paragraph 3].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
content: [SUPERSEDED] Draft v0.9 explored single-server cluster transitions without formal joint consensus intermediate states. In production deployment: This archival draft is retained exclusively for comparative distributed consensus research and regression testing. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 4, Paragraph 4].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
content: [HISTORICAL] Early draft formulations permitted followers to truncate uncommitted entries before receiving leader match confirmations. In production deployment: Do not apply Draft v0.9 configurations in production distributed state machine clusters. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 4, Paragraph 5].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
section: PostgreSQL 9.4 Legacy Row Security Proposal (Superseded Syntax) (Part 6)
content: [OBSOLETE SYNTAX] Early PostgreSQL 9.4 development proposals used experimental syntax ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW SECURITY without FORCE. In production deployment: PostgreSQL 16 rejects legacy 9.4 experimental syntax and mandates modern CREATE POLICY and ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 14, Paragraph 2].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
section: PostgreSQL 9.4 Legacy Row Security Proposal (Superseded Syntax) (Part 7)
content: [DEPRECATED BEHAVIOR] In early design drafts, table owners automatically bypassed row security checks without audit logging. In production deployment: Relying on obsolete 9.4 proposals leads to severe multi-tenant data leakage in modern PgBouncer pooled architectures. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 14, Paragraph 3].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
section: PostgreSQL 9.4 Legacy Row Security Proposal (Superseded Syntax) (Part 8)
content: [SUPERSEDED] Legacy proposals did not distinguish between USING filtering and WITH CHECK insertion constraints. In production deployment: Historical documentation entries are maintained for database migration regression benchmarks. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 14, Paragraph 4].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
section: PostgreSQL 9.4 Legacy Row Security Proposal (Superseded Syntax) (Part 1)
content: [CONFLICTING SYNTAX] Preliminary proposals lacked transaction-local set_config scoping, relying on connection-wide variables. In production deployment: PostgreSQL 16 rejects legacy 9.4 experimental syntax and mandates modern CREATE POLICY and ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 15, Paragraph 5].

In production deployment: Historical documentation entries are maintained for database migration regression benchmarks. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 27, Paragraph 5].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
section: PostgreSQL 9.4 Legacy Row Security Proposal (Superseded Syntax) (Part 5)
content: [CONFLICTING SYNTAX] Preliminary proposals lacked transaction-local set_config scoping, relying on connection-wide variables. In production deployment: PostgreSQL 16 rejects legacy 9.4 experimental syntax and mandates modern CREATE POLICY and ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 27, Paragraph 1].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
content: [SUPERSEDED DRAFT] TLS 1.3 Draft 21 utilized experimental HKDF label prefixes incompatible with RFC 8446 release standards. In production deployment: Modern TLS stacks explicitly reject Draft 21 handshakes as malformed protocol negotiation attempts. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 27, Paragraph 2].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
content: [INCOMPATIBLE CIPHERS] Draft 21 permitted transitional cipher suites that were removed before final publication of RFC 8446. In production deployment: Using Draft 21 key schedule derivation algorithms results in MAC verification failure on modern web servers. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 28, Paragraph 3].

content: [OBSOLETE STANDARD] NIST SP 800-63-2 mandated arbitrary periodic password rotation every 90 days, now formally banned by 800-63B. In production deployment: Compliance auditors referencing NIST SP 800-63-2 are non-compliant with modern NIST SP 800-63B Zero Trust security mandates. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 41, Paragraph 2].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
content: [DEPRECATED GUIDANCE] SP 800-63-2 enforced complex composition rules requiring uppercase, lowercase, digits, and special characters. In production deployment: Modern identity verification prioritizes password length, breached password screening, and multi-factor FIDO2 passkeys. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 41, Paragraph 3].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
content: [DISPROVEN PARADIGM] Studies proved 90-day rotation and composition rules cause predictable user transformations (e.g. Spring2024!). In production deployment: Archived for comparative analysis between legacy password policies and modern cryptographic standards. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 41, Paragraph 4].

documentTitle: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards
content: [SUPERSEDED] Knowledge-based authentication questions (security questions) permitted in 800-63-2 are strictly rejected in 800-63B. In production deployment: Compliance auditors referencing NIST SP 800-63-2 are non-compliant with modern NIST SP 800-63B Zero Trust security mandates. [Ref: Technical Specifications Archive and Superseded Standards, Chapter 41, Paragraph 5].
